newsitem.title: USA: US May trade gap widens, but Japan deficit cheers.
newsitem.headline: US May trade gap widens, but Japan deficit cheers.

text.p: A decline in exports after several months of steady growth and another solid rise in imports pushed the U.S. trade deficit to a wider-than-expected $10.23 billion in May.
But the politically sensitive gap with Japan showed a surprising decline, shrinking by 25 percent to $3.63 billion, its lowest level since June 1996.
"U.S. imports overall were quite strong," said John Rothfield, international economist at NationsBanc-CRT in Chicago.
"But I think the big decline with Japan is due to the fact that U.S. imports from that region suddenly became less attractive."

The dollar began its rapid pullback from multi-year highs against the yen in early May and Rothfield said this reversal may have contributed to the surprisingly good bilateral numbers with Japan during the month.
The Commerce Department reported that the overall deficit rose by 17.0 percent to $10.23 billion in May, above Wall Street expectations for a $9.18 billion shortfall.
The deficit for April was revised up to a wider $8.75 billion from a previously reported $8.36 billion.

Contributing to the wider deficit was a 0.8 percent decline in exports, a second consecutive decline after robust first quarter growth. Imports, which stood at record levels in April, rose for the seventh consecutive month, pusing up 1.0 percent to $87.47 billion.

Economists attributed the strong gains in imports to the robust U.S. economic growth experienced during the early part of 1997. They said the decline in exports was probably a temporary phenomenon which should reverse itself soon.
"If you look at the trend in exports, we've had a significant rise to a higher level and I don't think this is the beginning of a downtrend," said Rothfield.
The U.S. trade gaps with NAFTA partners Mexico and Canada worsened in May, but economists foresaw substantial improvement in those bilateral deficits in the months to come.
Both Mexico and Canada are showing strong growth at a time when the U.S. economy is showing signs of cooling off from unsustainably robust first quarter levels.

"You have a lot of strength in the Canadian economy, where people are worried about another tightening, and you have robust growth in Mexico," said Stephen Slifer, chief U.S. economist at Lehman Brothers.
Slifer was skeptical of the improvement with Japan, calling it "out of line" with recent Japanese trade data and predicting further deterioration in subsequent months.

The breakdown of goods showed that the value of crude oil imports rose to $4.60 billion in May from $4.29 billion despite a decline in the price of imported crude oil to an average $17.00 from $17.17 in April.
On the export side, declines were well dispersed between the advanced technology, agricultural, crude oil and manufacturing sectors.

Economists said that a downward revision to the March deficit would probably add a little to already robust first quarter growth figures, but said the report's implications for second quarter Gross Domestic Product numbers were negligible.
